sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A prepared statement separates SQL structure from data values. In Go, placeholders stay in the query while values are supplied as arguments to `ExecContext`, `QueryContext`, a prepared `*sql.Stmt`, or transaction methods.

The driver encodes each argument according to the database protocol instead of inserting its text into the SQL grammar. `db.PrepareContext` can create a reusable statement, although ordinary parameterized calls may already be prepared internally by the driver.

For example, a login lookup should use `WHERE email = $1` with the email as an argument. The text `x' OR true --` then remains one string value instead of becoming part of the WHERE clause.

Parameters do not validate business meaning, authorize access, make a query fast, or protect identifiers assembled into SQL. They solve the code-versus-data boundary for values; the rest still needs validation and access control.

Parameterize every untrusted value and use a reusable prepared statement only when its lifecycle and repeated execution provide a measured benefit. Keep dynamic identifiers behind an allow-list because placeholders represent values, not SQL keywords or column names.

sections.title: The core model: prepared statements and SQL parameters
sections.content:
prepared statements and SQL parameters is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

SQL injection occurs when data is allowed to alter the program represented by a query. Parameters prevent that by keeping the query structure fixed and transmitting each value separately. This remains useful even for values produced inside the service because it avoids manual escaping and type ambiguity. An explicit prepared statement is a performance and lifecycle tool, not the security requirement by itself: passing arguments to a normal context-aware query is still parameterized. Driver placeholder forms differ, such as `$1` or `?`, so portable code cannot assume one spelling. Identifiers are different because they are part of SQL grammar. If a report accepts a sort key, translate `created` to a literal trusted fragment such as `created_at`; never paste the raw request value. Finally, parameterization does not decide which rows a user is allowed to access. Authorization predicates and tenant boundaries must still be included and tested.

sections.title: prepared statements and SQL parameters example
sections.content:
~~~go
const lookup = `SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = $1`
var id int64
err := db.QueryRowContext(ctx, lookup, email).Scan(&id)

allowedSort := map[string]string{
    "created": "created_at",
    "name": "display_name",
}
column, ok := allowedSort[requestedSort]
if !ok { return ErrInvalidSort }
query := `SELECT id FROM users ORDER BY ` + column // trusted map value
~~~

sections.title: prepared statements and SQL parameters at a glance
sections.content:
| Input part | Placeholder? | Safe handling |
|---|---|---|
| Email, ID, date, amount | Yes | Pass as a query argument |
| Column or table name | No | Select from a fixed allow-list |
| ASC/DESC direction | No | Map a small enum to a literal |
| User authorization | Not solved by parameters | Add and test access predicates |
